tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the 1970s to the early 1990s', 1st paragraph (p. 235); Table 1, Renfroe row (p. 236)
tasks.extracted: Renfroe (1986), as summarized: of 610 samples of MDA or MDMA among 20,721 street drug samples sent to a Californian laboratory between 1972 and 1985, 12% (89 samples) were submitted under the names MDMA, MDM, Adam, XTC or ecstasy. The large majority of those 89 held MDMA or MDMA with MDA; only two held neither (a capsule from Honolulu with an amphetamine compound, and a largely empty plastic syringe from Miami labelled ecstasy/speed). Table 1 gives 97% (n=87) containing MDMA or MDA.

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy during the mid-1990s', 1st paragraph (begins p. 235, ends p. 236); Table 2, Spruit (2001) 1993–1997 row (p. 236)
tasks.extracted: Dutch Drug Information Monitoring System, as summarized from Spruit (2001): set up in 1992; samples were not collected systematically, most being brought in by individual people who wanted to know what a pill held; each pill was quick-tested and those not identified were sent for laboratory analysis (on average more than 100 pills a week). In each year from 1993 to 1996 about 48–60% of pills held MDMA alone, 12–20% MDEA alone, 2–5% MDA alone, 7–13% MDMA mixed with amphetamine or other drugs, 1–4% amphetamine alone and 2–7% amphetamine mixtures without MDMA; over 80% held an amphetamine-type drug; 6–17% held other drugs outside that class (hallucinogens such as LSD and ketamine, atropine, caffeine, paracetamol or unknown compounds). In 1997 44% held MDMA alone, 14% MDMA plus another drug, 24% MDA, MDEA or amphetamine and 18% other non-amphetamine drugs; the review links the dip to difficulty in obtaining the chemical precursor. The share holding MDMA rose to 75% in 1998 and 81% in 1999. Table 2 gives, for 1993–1997, 44–60% MDMA only, 9–25% MDEA or MDA only, 16–25% mixtures and 6–18% others.

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 1st paragraph; Table 3, Schifano (2000), Spruit (2001) and Palenicek et al. (2002) rows (p. 237)
tasks.extracted: Italy, as quoted from Schifano (2000): forensic laboratories had examined at least 20,000 tablets in five years; about 85–90% of tablets seized in the north-east held MDMA as the active ingredient, in amounts of 100–150 mg a tablet; MDA and MDEA were usually in the remainder, phenylbutanamine occasionally, and dummy tablets about 1% of the material (Table 3: 85–90% MDMA, 8–10% MDA or MDEA, 1% inactive, 1% others). Netherlands 1999: around 81% held MDMA (Table 3: 81% MDMA only, 19% all others). Czech Republic, Palenicek et al. (2002): 120 pills and capsules analysed between 1998 and 2002 (Table 3 says 1998–2001), over 80% held only MDMA; the rest held amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDEA, ketamine, ephedrine, MDA or mixtures (Table 3: more than 80% MDMA, 4% MDA, under 16% others and mixtures).

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Hansen et al. (2001) noted'; it continues on p. 238); Table 3, Winstock et al. row (p. 237)
tasks.extracted: Hansen et al. (2001), as summarized: people in Australia who used ecstasy and were surveyed between 1998 and 2000 estimated that about one tablet in every four or five was a dud; the review says this ratio is close to the more systematic survey data from Italy, the Netherlands and the Czech Republic. Winstock et al. (2001) surveyed 1151 dance clubbers in June 1999 about beliefs, consumption and perceptions of quality; Table 3 gives subjective reports of recent improvements in the quality of supplies.

tasks.locator: 'MDMA and ecstasy from the late 1990s to the early 2000s', 2nd paragraph, the part on p. 238 beginning 'The American website www.dancesafe.org' (the paragraph begins on p. 237); Table 3, Cole et al., Dancesafe and Ramsey (2003) rows (p. 237)
tasks.extracted: A US website, Dancesafe.org, listed tablets sent in for commercial analysis: about 175 tablets in 2002, of which 88% held MDMA alone or in combination and 4% held MDE or MDA (alone or in a combination without MDMA); Table 3 adds 4% others and 4% no identifiable drug. Ramsey et al. (2001): in samples from an amnesty bin at the entrance of a London dance venue, a high proportion of the tablets held MDMA and the powders were mostly amphetamine. Ramsey (2003), asked for later findings: the tablets in the bins were almost all MDMA. Cole et al. (2002): 136 tablets submitted to the Forensic Science Service in north-west England in 2001 all held MDMA by liquid chromatography.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has been described')
tasks.extracted: The review's own estimates of the share of ecstasy tablets holding MDMA: from the 1980s to the early 1990s around 90–98%, the remaining 2–10% generally MDA; in the mid to late 1990s between 50 and 80%, with around 5–30% holding MDA or MDEA and around 4–20% other drugs; in the late 1990s around 80–95% (citing Spruit and Winstock et al.); in the early 2000s values approaching 100% in the most recent surveys (citing Cole et al. and Ramsey).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 3rd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'These estimates can, however, only be seen as very approximate')
tasks.extracted: The review calls its estimates very approximate because the empirical evidence is limited: only three reports covered large samples over a long period (a US anonymous testing service, Renfroe 1986; the Dutch monitoring project, Spruit 2001; northern Italy, Schifano 2000), and the smaller surveys largely confirmed them. It adds that no study used a randomized sampling procedure; most samples were brought in by people who use drugs or came from amnesty bins; police seizures of large batches of uniform tablets may overestimate purity (Cole et al. 2002); and a US service charged $100 for each pill analysed (Baggott et al. 2000), far more than its street value, which probably led to a preponderance of atypical drugs.
tasks.quote: no study has employed a randomized sampling procedure

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'The non-equivalence of ecstasy and MDMA has practical consequences')
tasks.extracted: The review says that when a tablet holds MDA or MDEA, whose effects on brain chemistry are similar to those of MDMA, people would probably not notice any marked difference except possibly in how long the effect lasts or in subtle details of the experience (citing Hegadoren et al. 1999). In the Dutch data, even in the years with the lowest share of MDMA (1994 and 1997) the large majority of tablets still held MDMA, MDEA or MDA, and at other periods the match between ecstasy and MDMA was often around 90%.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'However, a substantial minority of ecstasy tablets')
tasks.extracted: The review states that a substantial minority of tablets held other compounds: between 1993 and 1997, 6–18% of Dutch samples held other drugs outside the amphetamine class. It says the effects of ketamine are so different from MDMA that taking it unknowingly could be extremely distressing, and reports that 4-methylthioamphetamine (4-MTA) was found in amnesty bins and, in the words of the authors it cites, had been implicated in four deaths in Britain and one in the Netherlands. A small proportion of tablets held weak substances (paracetamol, caffeine, placebo) and others held atropine, opiates, phenylbutanamine or dextromethorphan; the review says the acute effects of these could be unexpected and unpleasant.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'One intriguing question is why the supplies of ecstasy first became problematical')
tasks.extracted: The review says people who use ecstasy were fully aware of the quality problems of the mid-1990s and, when interviewed, can readily tell the occasions when they feel they have taken MDMA from their other experiences; jaw clenching, tooth grinding and the quality of mood changes are used to gauge the purity and strength of tablets, and one qualitative study described early nausea as a subjective sign. It adds that uncertainty over purity led many potential people to avoid illicit drugs, while regular ones often became more wary and took supplies only from friends. These are people's impressions; the review does not compare them with analyses of the tablets.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 7th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Dosage is another important topic', pp. 239–240)
tasks.extracted: Amounts of MDMA per tablet, as summarized: most Italian samples held 100–150 mg in 1995–2000 (Schifano 2000); UK annual averages were 90–102 mg between 1991 and 1995 and 73–88 mg between 1996 and 2001 (Cole et al. 2002). Small UK studies in the mid-1990s found amounts that were variable and often low: some tablets held 100–140 mg, others about 50 mg and some under 20 mg (Sherlock et al. 1999). In the Czech Republic tablets varied from 30 to 100 mg, with 152 mg and 0 mg (lactose) at the extremes (Palenicek et al. 2002). 80 white tablets from a large UK police seizure in 2001 held 73–89 mg, mean 79 mg (Cole et al. 2002). The Dutch monitoring met high-amount tablets occasionally in 1998. The review calls unknown amount a key area of uncertainty, says that high-amount tablets may be particularly dangerous for people taking MDMA for the first time because they could cause a severe serotonin syndrome reaction (no data given), and notes that two sources found no analytic evidence of toxic contaminants in MDMA batches (King 2000; Schifano 2000).

tasks.locator: 2.1 Complicating issues in generalising laboratory research to recreational human use, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The review notes that pills sold as ecstasy may not contain MDMA at all, so people developing regular or dependent use of ecstasy may not be taking MDMA, and that some or many pills may contain methamphetamine, so people may develop dependence on methamphetamine rather than, or as well as, MDMA. Some studies controlled statistically for other drug use, including methamphetamine, but that use was self-reported, not confirmed by laboratory testing.

tasks.locator: Table 1, rows Stone et al. to Bruno et al. (p. 4)
tasks.extracted: Population-based samples: Stone et al. (US National Household Surveys on Drug Abuse, 2000-2001; N 1199; six items matching DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria): 3.8% past year, among people who had started ecstasy within the previous two years. Von Sydow et al. (Germany, 1995-1999; representative sample aged 14-24; N 207; CIDI interview): 5.8% lifetime among people who had ever used ecstasy; less than 10% of those classed as lifetime dependent were past-year dependent at the 42-month follow-up. Wu et al. (US National Survey on Drug Use and Health, 2005; N 652; the same six hallucinogen items): 3.6% past year; another 11% reported one or two symptoms. Samples of sentinel populations: Parsons et al. (New York nightclub attendees aged 18-29 who had used ecstasy in the past 4 weeks; N 214; CIDI): 19% past year, with a median of 2.5 days of use in the past 4 months. Yen and Hsu (Taiwanese juvenile justice detainees who had used ecstasy; N 200): 22% past year. Self-selected sample: Bruno et al. (Australia, 2003-2004; N 1662; people using ecstasy at least monthly, recruited by purposive and snowball sampling; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 4 or more): 18% past month; among those screening positively, 49% used 1-2 times per week and 34% 1-2 times per month.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (continued), rows Cottler et al. to Thomasius et al. (p. 5)
tasks.extracted: Cottler et al. (US; adolescents and young adults in inpatient drug treatment and in the community, at least 5 lifetime occasions of use; N 52; computerised CIDI module): 43% lifetime; the most common symptoms were continued use despite problems (63%) and withdrawal (59%), and all dependent participants had tolerance or withdrawal. Hanson and Luciana (US students and community members; N 26; DSM-IV abuse or dependence): the prevalence cell reads N = 2 LT while the details column says 14 met the criteria. Scheier et al. (US and Australia; N 639; modified CIDI): no prevalence given, mean 227 lifetime pills. Topp et al. (Australia, 1997; N 185; CIDI): 64% lifetime; the authors questioned how withdrawal symptoms were endorsed. Tossman (Germany, 2002; N 195; people who used ecstasy and/or methamphetamine in the past year): 16%, timeframe not specified. Yacoubian et al. (Washington rave attendees; N 154; a screening scale): 17% lifetime, 'probable' dependence. Thomasius et al. (Germany; rave attendees with at least 250 lifetime tablets, mean 794; N 59; clinical interview rated by clinical psychologists): 73% lifetime.

tasks.locator: Table 1 (continued), Winstock et al. row, and footnote; 3.2 Studies of ecstasy dependence among users, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 6)
tasks.extracted: Winstock et al. (UK, 1999; readers of a dance music magazine who had ever used ecstasy; N 1106; Severity of Dependence Scale score of 5 or more): 17%, with a footnote that the timeframe was not specified; mean 160 lifetime occasions of use; tolerance and continued use despite problems with health, work or relationships were reported by more than half of the sample. Section 3.2: few studies have examined dependence among people who use ecstasy; all used instruments designed for other drugs, and just one (of a non-representative sample) involved clinician or psychiatric assessment. Topp et al. (1997): 64% of 185 people who regularly used ecstasy met lifetime criteria, typically during their heaviest use period, when 66% were using 1-2 times per week and 25% between 1 and 3 days per month; the authors questioned whether the withdrawal items separated comedown effects from dysphoria that eases with further use.

tasks.locator: 3.2, the paragraph beginning 'Two large survey samples of dependence' and the paragraph beginning 'Studies of dependence among ecstasy users in representative general population samples are limited'
tasks.extracted: Two large samples used the five-item Severity of Dependence Scale, which measures compulsion to use: in the UK survey of 1106 dance-magazine readers 17% screened positive for lifetime ecstasy dependence, and in the Australian interview-based study of 1662 people who regularly used ecstasy, 18% screened positive; of these 49% used ecstasy 1-2 times per week, 34% used 1-3 times per month and only 2% (n = 7) were using at least every second day, and financial, legal and work harms, sexual risk, overdose and help seeking were more common than among those who screened negative, independent of problematic methamphetamine use. In general population samples a German study found that past-year ecstasy/hallucinogen/stimulant dependence among all young adults was 0.4%; a US study found that 4% of people who had used ecstasy in the past year met DSM-IV hallucinogen dependence criteria (another 11% reported one or two symptoms) (Wu et al.), and 3.82% of those who had started ecstasy in the previous two years had developed dependence (Stone et al.); some have argued that grouping ecstasy with the hallucinogens in DSM-IV may not fit the behavioural data.

tasks.locator: 3.3 The structure of ecstasy dependence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (the 3rd begins on p. 7 and ends on p. 8)
tasks.extracted: Two studies of the structure of the symptoms, both in Australian samples (one also in US samples): Topp et al. (1997) found for ecstasy, unlike alcohol, cannabis, cocaine and opioids, two separate components, compulsive use (use despite problems, giving up activities, unsuccessful attempts to stop, withdrawal, excessive time spent) and escalating use (tolerance, and using more or for longer than intended); Bruno et al. (2009) found two related factors with the same names for the Severity of Dependence Scale. The review concludes that the dependence syndrome may not be of the same nature as for alcohol, opioids and amphetamine, and that behavioural reinforcement or learning may play a part for some people.

tasks.locator: 3.4 The course of ecstasy dependence; 3.5 Treatment seeking for ecstasy-related problems, 1st paragraph (p. 8)
tasks.extracted: Course: only one study has followed people who met DSM-IV criteria for ecstasy dependence (von Sydow et al., 2002; a German population-based study of young adults with a mean follow-up of just over three years): 93% were no longer dependent at follow-up; 50% were no longer using the drug at all, and of the 43% still using, the majority did not meet criteria for a use disorder; the authors suggested that ecstasy dependence might be a transient phenomenon. Treatment: routine data in Australia show very small numbers of treatment episodes for ecstasy (less than 1% of all episodes), consistent with surveys finding that treatment seeking is infrequent even among people who report concerns about their use.

tasks.locator: 3.6 Limitations of existing human evidence, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; 4 Summary and implications, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 8)
tasks.extracted: Limitations: the studies are extremely heterogeneous in assessment methods and samples, which makes meta-analysis inappropriate; dependence was typically assessed by self-report without clinician verification, usually as lifetime retrospective reports; despite relatively infrequent use even at their heaviest, people very commonly reported dependence symptoms, and it is unclear whether participants understood the questions as the investigators intended; the prevalence cannot be extrapolated to all people who use ecstasy because most studies recruited people with recent use by convenience or snowball sampling; information on the natural history comes mostly from retrospective reports of convenience samples. Summary: the review judges the evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome to be restricted in how much was studied and in how it was studied (see the quotation); animal evidence suggests MDMA may be a less potent reinforcer than other drugs but still has dependence potential; some people report problems controlling their use and concern about it, but there is a notable lack of case reports of severe withdrawal, which suggests physical symptoms play a more limited role than psychological ones; tolerance and withdrawal have been reported, mostly in questionnaires designed for other drugs; treatment presentations are uncommon compared with the prevalence of use but do occur.
tasks.quote: The evidence for an ecstasy dependence syndrome is limited in both scope and design.

tasks.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph (p. 1442)
tasks.extracted: Recruitment: people who had taken MDMA in the past year were recruited from the psychiatry departments of two general hospitals and from help centres for people with drug problems in Brussels and Flanders, Belgium, between December 2004 and February 2006; all took part voluntarily with written consent. Because substance use is mostly not limited to one drug, an experienced psychiatrist interviewed each person about current and past drug use (the paper does not report what the interviews found). People with a history of ergot-derived drugs, Chinese herbs, appetite-suppressant drugs, intravenous drugs or any drug known to induce valve disease were excluded, as were people with any past cardiac disease, congenital or degenerative valve disease (including mitral or tricuspid prolapse) found on echocardiography, or poor image quality. Controls were age- and sex-matched students who answered advertisements and reported no drug use, with the same exclusions.

tasks.locator: Methods, 3rd to 5th paragraphs; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1443)
tasks.extracted: Examinations were done by experienced sonographers who were not told the person's identity; images were stored, randomized and read blind by one sonographer and one independent observer, whose agreement on the FDA criteria was excellent (kappa above 0.9) and whose data were used. Valve disease was defined by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) criteria for appetite-suppressant-induced valve disease: mitral regurgitation of moderate or greater severity (2/4 or more) or aortic regurgitation of mild or greater severity (1/4 or more); Fisher's exact test was used for the FDA score. Results: 33 people who took MDMA and 29 controls were selected, none with a history of cardiac disease; 4 people in the MDMA group were excluded after scanning (3 for inadequate image quality, 1 for mitral and tricuspid prolapse), leaving 29; all had used MDMA for at least 6 months. 8 people (28%) who took MDMA met the FDA criteria and none of the controls (p = 0.0045); mitral, aortic and tricuspid regurgitation and shape abnormalities were more often seen in the MDMA group (Table 1).

tasks.locator: Table 1, Demographics and Echocardiographic findings
tasks.extracted: Controls against subjects taking MDMA (n = 29 against 33 for demographics, 29 against 29 for echocardiography). Demographics: women 13 (45%) against 15 (45%); mean age 25.6 (SD 2.6) against 24.3 (SD 3.1) years, p = 0.10; MDMA use in the MDMA group 3.6 (SD 6.7) tablets a week for 6.1 (SD 3.4) years. Echocardiography: mitral insufficiency 2/4 or more 0 against 4 (14%), p = 0.11; mitral regurgitant area ratio 5% (SD 1.3) against 12% (SD 9.8), p < 0.007; mitral restrictive motion 0 against 7 (24%), p = 0.01; mitral strand 0 against 1 (3%); aortic insufficiency 1/4 or more 0 against 4 (14%), p = 0.11; aortic strand 0 against 5 (17%), p = 0.05; tricuspid regurgitation 2/4 or more 0 against 13 (45%), p < 0.001; tricuspid regurgitant area ratio 9% (SD 4.5) against 19% (SD 9.5), p < 0.001; tricuspid restrictive motion 1 (3%) against 5 (17%), p = 0.19; pulmonary regurgitation 1/4 or more 10 (34%) against 14 (48%), p = 0.42. The table also prints relative risks with intervals whose basis is not explained; they are not used here.

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'In the MDMA group, subjects with valvular regurgitation')
tasks.extracted: In the MDMA group, people with mitral or tricuspid regurgitation of 2/4 or more, or any aortic regurgitation, had on average taken more tablets in total (943, SD 1,162) than those with lower grades (242, SD 212), p = 0.03; the group sizes and the way the cumulative number was calculated are not given.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 1444)
tasks.extracted: The authors state that this is the first report of valve disease in young adults using or having used MDMA, that valve disease in young adults is very unusual and was not found in their controls, and that strands were seen in the MDMA group and not in the controls. They describe a cell-culture study (Setola et al.) in which MDMA bound to and activated human 5-HT2B receptors and caused prolonged growth responses in human valve cells, and suggest that this may explain valve disease with intermittent use; the present study did not test the mechanism.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 6th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'Although in our study, regurgitations were hemodynamically most often mild to moderate') and 7th paragraph (the paragraph beginning 'This study has some limitations')
tasks.extracted: The authors write that the regurgitations were most often mild to moderate in their effect on blood flow. Limitations they state: MDMA is illegal and people were difficult to recruit, so the study is relatively small; information about the amount of use came from interrogating the people; there were no echocardiographic data from before MDMA use because a prospective evaluation was not possible for ethical reasons; and there is no pathologic evidence of the valve abnormalities because no valve surgery was needed. They say that further studies should help define the clinical significance and extent of the findings. (The paper also calls its findings of great clinical importance and suggests endocarditis prophylaxis; no data in the paper test those statements.)
tasks.quote: There were no echocardiographic data available before MDMA use

tasks.locator: Methods, Toxicological analysis (1st and 2nd paragraphs), Cohort selection, Data analysis, and Table I (p. 220)
tasks.extracted: Cases came from the Australian National Coroners Information System: all closed Victorian cases between January 2002 and December 2008 with a positive, quantified MDMA result above 0.02 mg/L in postmortem blood (femoral vein blood where possible, to limit redistribution). Toxicology used immunoassay screening and confirmation by gas chromatography with mass spectrometry, with a lower limit of quantitation for MDMA of 0.02 mg/L. The authors assessed each case's other drugs and the likelihood of a toxic reaction, including the risk of serotonin toxicity. Table I groups the drugs found: major interaction, moclobemide (a reversible MAO-A inhibitor; hypertensive crisis and serotonin toxicity); moderate interaction, dothiepin (a tricyclic antidepressant), amphetamine and derivatives (amphetamine, methamphetamine, MDA, MDEA), tramadol, venlafaxine and cocaine (serotonin toxicity), and methadone and fluoxetine (CYP2D6 inhibitors, raising MDMA concentrations); minor interaction, doxylamine and the SSRIs citalopram, sertraline and fluvoxamine.

tasks.locator: Methods, Data analysis, the paragraphs beginning 'Cases demonstrating a risk of ST' and ''Major' interactions were those' (p. 223); Results, Basic characteristics, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 223)
tasks.extracted: Cases showing a risk of serotonin toxicity or another adverse drug reaction were examined more closely, and other cases (MDMA alone, or with drugs unlikely to produce a reaction) were excluded from further investigation because the cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only. Cases were grouped as major, moderate or minor interaction by risk of drug toxicity from a drug-information database and other references; fluoxetine and paroxetine were counted as moderate because their strong inhibition of the enzyme CYP2D6 can raise MDMA concentrations, and the weak inhibition by sertraline and citalopram was taken as unlikely to contribute to a fatal reaction. Results: 106 cases between 2002 and 2008 with quantified MDMA above the minimum level, among 14,682 coroners' cases that had full toxicological testing; 83 (78%) were male and 64 (60%) died by external injury (for example hangings, motor vehicle crashes); ages 17 to 48, median 25. Of the 106, 4 were a major risk, 10 moderate and 5 minor (Table II); these 19 were examined in detail. The other 87 were MDMA alone or with MDA as metabolite (20), MDMA with ethanol (34) or MDMA with other drugs not likely to cause an adverse drug reaction (33).
tasks.quote: this cohort focused on toxic drug combinations only

tasks.locator: Table II, the 19 cases (pp. 221-223): columns Cause of Death and Autopsy Findings and Postmortem Blood Drug Concentration
tasks.extracted: Table II lists each of the 19 cases by group with sex and age, cause of death and autopsy findings, the drugs found in postmortem blood with concentrations, and the specimen site and postmortem interval. Group 1 (cases 1 to 4): all four had moclobemide. Groups 2 (cases 5 to 14) and 3 (cases 15 to 19) held, besides the drugs that defined the group, combinations of methamphetamine, amphetamine, opioids (codeine, morphine, methadone, tramadol, 6-MAM), benzodiazepines and their metabolites (diazepam, alprazolam, temazepam, oxazepam, nordiazepam, 7-aminoflunitrazepam), other antidepressants (dothiepin, venlafaxine, fluoxetine, sertraline, citalopram, fluvoxamine, mirtazapine), paracetamol, ibuprofen, cannabis (THC) and ethanol, and in single cases ketamine, p-methoxyamphetamine, olanzapine, metoclopramide and frusemide. Editors' tally of the table's rows, cases with at least one: methamphetamine or amphetamine 15 (methamphetamine 14, amphetamine 7); antidepressant 13 (moclobemide 4, others 9); opioid 12 (11 without 6-MAM; methadone 5, codeine 5, morphine 5, tramadol 1, 6-MAM 3); benzodiazepine or metabolite 8 (cases 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 14, 15, 19); benzodiazepine or opioid 14; paracetamol or ibuprofen 4; cannabis 5; ethanol 3; blood MDMA 0.05 mg/L or less in 5 cases (6, 8, 9, 13, 14). Cause of death: drug toxicity alone in 12 (cases 1-5, 7, 9, 10, 12, 15, 18, 19), injury plus combined drug toxicity in 2 (13, 17), and drowning, train impact, hemorrhagic shock, hanging or carbon monoxide poisoning in the other 5.

tasks.locator: Results, Toxicology findings in the 19 cases of interest, 1st paragraph (begins p. 223, ends p. 224), 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 224)
tasks.extracted: The 19 cases were mostly male (14), aged 21 to 45 (median 28). The four Group 1 cases all involved moclobemide, with postmortem blood MDMA 1.0 to 2.6 mg/L (median 1.85); clinical symptoms of serotonin toxicity were reported by a paramedic or physician in three of them (cases 1 to 3). Group 2 (10 cases) had fluoxetine, venlafaxine, methadone, dothiepin and tramadol with MDMA, and also paramethoxyamphetamine and methamphetamine, with MDMA 0.02 to 3.5 mg/L (median 0.07). Group 3 (5 cases) involved citalopram, fluvoxamine, sertraline and/or doxylamine, with MDMA 0.2 to 1.4 mg/L (median 0.2).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph and the paragraph beginning 'In this cohort, ST was reported'
tasks.extracted: Four cases involved moclobemide with MDMA, a combination associated with serotonin toxicity; the authors note that moclobemide was originally marketed as a safer alternative to older MAO inhibitors and that a search across Australia would probably find more such deaths. Serotonin toxicity was reported from symptoms witnessed before death in three cases (1 to 3); despite the possibility in many other cases, including moderate-risk cases with serotonin-active drugs, it was not reported. The authors consider it more likely that it was overlooked, or that the lack of symptoms before death (for example when the person was found dead) prevented a diagnosis, than that it did not occur.

tasks.locator: Discussion, the paragraph beginning 'In the Copeland et al. study' (begins p. 224, ends p. 225); Limitations paragraph; Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 225)
tasks.extracted: In many postmortem cases the source of the drugs, licit or illicit, remains unknown unless a medicolegal investigation specifies it, which was unusual here; witness statements in a number of cases, including two of the moclobemide cases with fatal serotonin toxicity, suggested that the person may have obtained the medicines from a friend or family member. Limitations the authors state: postmortem redistribution may alter drug concentrations (some specimens were taken days after death, for example six days in case 18, or from non-peripheral sites such as cavity blood in case 10); missing information, including the source of the drugs (prescribing information) and clinical data such as temperature; people are usually found dead, so symptoms go unreported; and concentrations of drugs that produce tolerance, such as morphine, are hard to interpret. Conclusions: some people who use ecstasy may combine pharmaceutical drugs to strengthen the effect or ease the comedown, but this appeared to be a limited practice in Victoria in 2002-2008; people taking medicines for treatment who occasionally use ecstasy are at risk, particularly if unaware of interactions; many of the deaths were apparently unintentional drug toxicity, so knowledge of these interactions is likely to be limited.

tasks.locator: Table 3, Schifano et al. (2003) row (p. 237)
tasks.extracted: Parrott's Table 3, as summarized: Schifano et al. (2003), UK 1997-2000, toxicological analyses of 75 deaths attributed to ecstasy, XTC, MDMA or MDA: 91% MDMA, 9% MDA, other drugs also found in 93% of cases, mainly opiates and sedatives.

tasks.locator: Methods > Study design, 1st paragraph; Methods > Subjects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Methods > Study drug, 1st paragraph (p. 577, left column into right column)
tasks.extracted: Pooled analysis of nine double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover studies, all at the University Hospital Basel, in 166 psychiatrically screened, healthy European or Caucasian adults aged 18 to 45 (mean 24.5, SD 4), mostly recruited on the university campus and paid, equal numbers of women and men. 30 people took a single 75 mg dose; 136 took 125 mg (24 once; 112 twice, once alone and once after another drug, at least seven days apart, the pretreatment sessions being analysed separately). This paper analyses the 166 sessions of MDMA alone against placebo. Exclusions: psychiatric disorder, physical illness, illicit drug use more than five times in a lifetime (past cannabis excepted), any in the last two months or during the study (urine tests before sessions). Fifty-nine people had tried a drug 1 to 5 times, 34 of them MDMA 1 to 4 times. The study drug was MDMA hydrochloride from a pharmaceutical supplier, in capsules.

tasks.locator: Methods > Pharmacodynamic measures, 1st paragraph (4 people left out of the timing analysis) and 2nd paragraph (p. 578, left column)

tasks.extracted: MDMA alone raised blood pressure, heart rate and body temperature (Table 2). Over the 166 sessions: systolic above 160 mm Hg in 54 people (33%) and above 180 in 7 (4%); heart rate above 100 in forty-eight people (29%); ear temperature above 38 degrees Celsius in 32 (19%), up to 39.1. tasks.locator: Discussion > 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 584, right column)
tasks.extracted: The authors read the vital-sign changes, in people at rest, as similar to moderate physical activity; transient systolic pressure above 180 mm Hg was seen in 5% of those given 125 mg, with no other sign of a hypertensive crisis (severe headache, shortness of breath or nosebleed); an earlier analysis of 74 people from laboratory studies had found systolic pressure at or above 160 in 32% and at or above 180 in 9%. Temperatures did not rise above 39.1 degrees Celsius. No controlled clinical study of MDMA has reported a temperature above 40, which the authors suggest may be because participants had moderate single doses at rest, were well hydrated and were not in a hot or crowded place, unlike some recreational settings.

tasks.extracted: Onset of effects 33 minutes, peak 1.6 hours, duration 4.2 hours; the 75 and 125 mg doses did not differ in how long effects lasted. The authors attribute the short duration of effect, compared with the long time MDMA stays in the blood, to acute pharmacological tolerance, so that effects decline while MDMA is still in the body, and argue that adding more MDMA might not relevantly prolong the effect and may increase adverse effects (citing a separate study of second doses). This is their interpretation, not a result of this study: every session used a fixed dose.

tasks.extracted: A research assistant was always present with the participants in the laboratory, similar to a therapy session. Only psychiatrically healthy, mostly young people were included. tasks.locator: Methods, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, last paragraph (p. 434, left column into right column)
tasks.extracted: Retrospective series. All documented telephone enquiries to the London centre of the UK National Poisons Information Service from December 1993 to November 1995 were screened for MDMA use complicated by serum sodium below 130 mmol/l, advice cases to March 1996 were added, and a further fatal case was included. Of a mean 13 762 enquiries a month, 135 (1.0%) concerned ecstasy; over the 28-month study period 17 cases were identified (0.4% of all enquiries about ecstasy, a share of telephone calls and not a risk): seven male and 10 female, aged 15 to 26. Table 1 covers the 15 who recovered. Analytical confirmation of MDMA ingestion was obtained in eight cases. Eight patients were known to have ingested a large amount of non-alcoholic or alcoholic fluid; for five the history of fluid ingestion was not available. The pattern was uniform: vomiting and disturbed behaviour, then drowsiness, agitation and, in 10 patients, seizures; drowsiness, a mute state and disorientation lasted up to 3 days; clinical findings did not necessarily reflect the size of the fall in sodium; in six patients blood and urine tests were consistent with inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). In the two who died, symptoms of cerebral oedema began within 5 hours of one tablet, and in both an excessive amount of fluid had been drunk.

They add that the mechanism by which MDMA causes this secretion remains to be established, and that acute stress and excessive visual and sound stimuli might contribute, as might nicotine (whether the patients smoked is not known).

tasks.locator: Limitations, 1st to 4th paragraphs (starts p. 168, right column; ends p. 169, right column)
tasks.extracted: Poison-centre data are passive reporting, subject to reporting bias. The authors say they may have missed cases and underestimated complications; that referral bias may produce spectrum bias, the series representing the more severe outcomes and possibly overestimating how often low sodium and poor outcomes occur; that exposure rests on a history from the patient or a witness and may include other substances sold as ecstasy; that laboratory confirmation of MDMA was lacking in a significant share and no gas chromatography with mass spectrometry was reported; that no sodium was recorded in 65.5% of cases, the timing of the sodium was not consistent, and low sodium may be relatively benign and self-correcting in some; and that differing body build, kidney function, hydration, coingestions and behaviour limit conclusions about how likely a given population is to develop low sodium.

tasks.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 3 (p. 1855, right column)
tasks.extracted: As described in the review, second-hand: symptomatic low sodium (usually below 130 mEq/L) was first described by Maxwell and colleagues in 1993 and more than 25 separate case reports have been published since; sodium on presentation ranged from 101 to 130 mEq/L, and the vast majority of cases were in females aged 15 to 30 who took a single dose of ecstasy. The review attributes excess water intake in part to a harmful response to overheating (chill-out areas with free or cheap water or low-solute drinks), together with amphetamine-induced dry mouth and thirst; whether ecstasy gives a primary drive to drink is not known but has been hypothesized. Editors' count of Table 3: 32 published cases, 27 labelled F, 1 W and 4 M, 16 deaths, 15 recoveries and 1 not available; 10 rows are taken from the California series (reference 82 in the review).

tasks.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 2nd paragraph, the case report (starts p. 1855, right column; continues p. 1856, left column)
tasks.extracted: As described in the review: an 18-year-old woman came to an emergency department soon after taking five tablets of ecstasy, with severe headache and thirst and a serum sodium of 136 mEq/L; she then drank 1700 ml of water, her headache worsened and the repeat sodium was 130 mEq/L, with urine osmolality 335 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 101 mEq/L and plasma arginine vasopressin 33.7 pmol/L (normal below 5.6). The review reasons that ready fluids, severe thirst and advice to drink copiously are likely not enough on their own, because the kidney can usually excrete free water faster than it is taken in, so the kidney's water excretion must also be impaired, as the raised urine osmolality and vasopressin in this and other cases suggest.

tasks.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, paragraphs on vasopressin secretion and on sweat sodium (p. 1856, left and right columns)
tasks.extracted: As described in the review: MDMA has been shown in case reports and controlled settings to induce vasopressin secretion. Henry and colleagues gave 40 mg (against a common street dose of 100 mg) to eight healthy volunteers and found vasopressin rose within 1 to 2 hours (from a baseline range of 1.14 to 1.88 pmol/L to 2.46 to 9.16) with a slight fall in serum sodium; several other controlled studies are said to show a rise within 1 to 2 hours, and the rise is said to correlate negatively with MDMA levels, suggesting a metabolite. Sweat sodium loss is judged likely marginal, the majority of case reports lack significant hyperthermia, and the review concludes that increased water ingestion with urinary water retention is the main driving force. None of these primary studies was read here.

tasks.extracted: Of the 17 patients, 10 were female and 7 male; both who died were female (15 and 18 years). This is a description of cases reported to a poisons service, with no comparison group and no information on how many women and men took MDMA or were tested.

tasks.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, 1st paragraph; Table 3 (p. 1855, right column)
tasks.extracted: As described in the review, second-hand: the vast majority of the more than 25 published case reports were in females aged 15 to 30 who took a single dose. Editors' count of Table 3 (32 published cases): 27 labelled F, 1 W and 4 M; 10 rows are taken from the California series (reference 82 in the review) and a 15-year-old female with sodium 125 who died appears to be the first UK death, so the tabulated cases are not independent of the two series.

tasks.locator: Hyponatremia and Ecstasy, the paragraph beginning 'Acutely, the fall in serum sodium' (p. 1857, left column)
tasks.extracted: As described in the review, second-hand: a review of published case reports and series found more than 85% of symptomatic low-sodium patients were female; the California study is said to have documented that women had a significantly higher incidence of symptomatic low sodium, coma and death; the review says the sex difference does not reflect more women taking ecstasy, because other complications are more frequent in men; and it offers oestrogen effects on the brain's sodium pump and on cerebral blood vessels, and lower muscle mass and body weight in women, as possible reasons. Editors' note: the California study is cited in the review as reference 49, which in the review's list is a different 1998 case report (the California paper is reference 82), and its own Table 3 gives death odds ratios of 1.39 (0.22 to 8.65) in women and 1.85 (0.16 to 21.70) in men, both intervals including 1.

tasks.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, 1st and 2nd paragraphs and Table 2 (p. 1854, left and right columns)
tasks.extracted: As described in the review: acute kidney injury has been associated with ecstasy, mostly in case reports, so the absolute incidence cannot be determined. The first case report, in 1992, was a person who took three doses of ecstasy at a rave and developed kidney injury attributed to muscle breakdown (rhabdomyolysis) after seizures and possibly a direct toxic effect on muscle, with disseminated intravascular coagulation. The review calls non-traumatic rhabdomyolysis the most common scenario and says that in the majority of such cases people had been exerting themselves to excessive levels with inadequate hydration, compounded by impaired temperature regulation and very high temperature; creatine kinase can reach 100,000 U/L or more, and volume depletion and low blood pressure add to the injury from myoglobin. Table 2 lists causes: muscle breakdown (from overheating, extreme exertion, or an unknown direct toxicity), necrotizing vasculitis (rare case reports), bladder-neck obstruction (one case report), malignant hypertension, proximal tubule dysfunction (one case report) and volume depletion.
tasks.quote: the absolute incidence of this complication cannot be determined

tasks.locator: Acute Kidney Injury Associated with Ecstasy, paragraphs on proximal tubule dysfunction, liver failure and vasculitis (p. 1854, right column); paragraph on bladder-neck dysfunction and malignant hypertension (p. 1855, left column)
tasks.extracted: As described in the review: transient glycosuria, phosphaturia and solute diuresis in an 18-year-old (a single report; mechanism unknown, with injury to proximal tubules shown in a rat model); acute liver failure with kidney injury through the hepatorenal syndrome; necrotizing vasculitis with end-stage kidney disease in a 30-year-old man 10 days after use, and graft loss from necrotizing vasculitis in both kidneys of a donor with recent ecstasy use; obstruction from bladder-neck dysfunction; kidney injury after accelerated or malignant hypertension. The review says no case report of kidney injury after ecstasy has had a kidney biopsy that could show a direct toxic effect, and that attributing causation to ecstasy in the vasculitis cases is difficult because the people may have used other substances.

tasks.locator: Conclusions, 1st paragraph (p. 1857, right column)
tasks.extracted: The review concludes that ecstasy use is associated with both kidney injury and low blood sodium, and that most of the episodes of kidney injury are due to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis associated with rhabdomyolysis.

tasks.locator: Section 4 > Clinical hyperthermia and its treatment, 2nd paragraph (p. 5, left column into right column)
tasks.extracted: As summarized by the review (Henry and colleagues, 1992, UK poisons unit, 1990 and 1991): 7 deaths with overheating, admission temperatures 40 to 43 degrees Celsius; the most severe cases showed overheating, disseminated intravascular coagulation, muscle breakdown and acute renal failure; the authors noted these severe reactions did not reflect high dose levels, with plasma MDMA from 0.11 to 1.26 mg/l, and other drugs were reported in only one case; four further severe non-fatal cases had temperatures around 40 degrees.

tasks.locator: Methods > Blood sampling and EOS visit, 1st paragraph (p. 578, right column); Results > Effects of MDMA on kidney and liver function (p. 582, left column); Table 4 (p. 583)
tasks.extracted: Kidney tests in 164 of the 166 healthy volunteers (data missing for two), at screening and at an end-of-study visit on average 29 (SD 22) days after the last of one or two doses of MDMA (the Results text gives 30 +/- 22), 88 (SD 50) days between the visits: creatinine 74 (SD 13) against 73 (SD 12) micromoles per litre and estimated glomerular filtration rate 122 (SD 22) against 125 (SD 24) mL/min, neither significantly different. Liver enzymes were also similar, apart from a small fall in gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase.

tasks.locator: Discussion > 'The present study has limitations' paragraph (p. 585, right column)
tasks.extracted: The authors write that laboratory markers of liver and kidney function were assessed only at the end of the study, on average one month after the last dose, which does not exclude short-lasting transient changes; that only healthy, mostly young people were included; and that 166 sessions of MDMA alone (278 with or without a pretreatment) were too small to exclude infrequent or rare adverse events.
